headline: Beavertail bunker push blues onto the ledges, doormats stack the East Passage
subhead: Peanut bunker are pouring off the rocks from Brenton Point to Sakonnet, and everything with teeth is following them in.
body_markdown:
Walked out onto the ledges below Beavertail Tuesday morning and the water was nervous before I even made a cast — peanut bunker stacked three deep against the rocks, silversides skittering on top of them, and something big pushing from underneath. That's the tell this time of year. When the bait gets that jumpy right against structure, you don't need a fish finder, you need a rod in your hand and your feet already wet.

That bunker push has been the whole story along the south shore this week, from Brenton Point down through the Dumplings and into the mouth of the Sakonnet. We flagged this pattern last week — said the bluefish bite was entirely bait-driven, that wherever the bunker re-formed after a blow, the blues would show within hours — and that's exactly what's playing out. Second Beach had a solid blitz Thursday evening, gulls working tight over busting bait, blues in the 3-6 pound range crushing everything from Hopkins jigs to topwater poppers. Sakonnet Point has had the same show on and off, best right at first light before the boat traffic pushes through. If you see the bunker balled up tight against a ledge, don't wait — that window can close in twenty minutes once the blues move through and scatter them.

Striped bass are playing the game they always play in early August — deep and quiet on structure through the day, up and hunting in the low light. The rocks off Beavertail and around the Dumplings are holding fish 25 to 40 feet down, and daytime action there means dropping bucktails or diamond jigs and working them slow off the bottom. But dawn and dusk change everything. I've had my best action swimming a 3-ounce bucktail with a white or chartreuse curl-tail trailer right along the base of the ledges at Sakonnet Point on the last two hours of the incoming, right as the light starts to go flat. Night eelers working the Sakonnet River bridges and the pilings around Jamestown have been doing well too — nothing giant, mostly 26 to 34 inches, but steady enough to make the late shift worth it.

Fluke are about as good as they get right now, which lines up with what the whole region is seeing this time of year. The East Passage rip off the Newport Bridge has been holding doormat-class fish in 30 to 45 feet, and drifting the edge of that channel with a white Gulp Swimming Mullet on a 3/4-ounce bucktail has produced fish to 6 pounds for me twice this week. Sakonnet River mouth is fishing the same way — work the channel edges on the dropping tide, keep the boat moving slow, and don't be afraid to bounce bottom hard. The warm, stable water has these fish feeding aggressively on the move, and that pattern should hold as long as this settled weather sticks around.

Tog are a mixed bag right now, and I'll be honest about it — midsummer isn't when this fishery shines. The deep ledges off Beavertail and the rockpiles around Gould Island are holding fish, but they're tucked into the cracks and cooler pockets in 35 to 50 feet, and you're working for every bite. Green crabs on a jig head, dropped right into the crevices on the slack tide, have picked at a few keepers, but it's slow, patient fishing more than a bite you can count on. I'd treat it as scouting for the fall run rather than a primary target right now. Scup, on the other hand, are an easy, reliable pick off almost any rocky point from Newport to Napatree — bloodworms or squid strips on a high-low rig in 15 to 25 feet will keep a rod bent all afternoon if that's the kind of day you're after.

Albies haven't shown yet, and I want to be straight about that rather than tease something that isn't here. Every year guys start asking about Napatree and Watch Hill the first week of August, and every year I tell them the same thing — it's early. That first push into the breachways usually doesn't happen until temperature breaks start stacking up in September, though with squid starting to show around the region and the water holding steady, this is worth watching closer than usual. I'll be checking the rock at the tip of Napatree and the mouth of the Weekapaug breachway on my evening walks, looking for that nervous water and diving birds that tell you they've arrived early.

Looking ahead, the tides are sliding toward neap around the 5th and 6th, which means current everywhere from the East Passage to the Sakonnet River is going to soften up. That calls for lighter jigs and slower retrieves on the fluke grounds, and it usually means the bass tuck tighter to structure and feed in shorter windows. If I had one day to fish this week, I'd take the last two hours of daylight at Sakonnet Point on the incoming — bunker still pushing, bass and blues both still working that structure, and enough light left to see the water turn.
